newsitem.title: USA: US economy likely to slow through 1997 - Fed sources.
newsitem.headline: US economy likely to slow through 1997 - Fed sources.

text.p: The U.S. economy is expected to slow down through 1997 after reaching a sizzling growth rate in the first quarter, according to three sources at the Federal Reserve.

"I would expect that the economy would slow down, that this rate of growth would not persist over the year. But the very exact time (when the slowdown will occur) is still hard to say," a Fed source told Reuters on Wednesday.
Another Federal Reserve source agreed, adding that strong consumer spending was one of the main factors behind the strong growth earlier in the year.
"The growth rate in the first quarter was huge, really remarkable and again driven by consumer spending ... It would really be hard to sustain that," the second Fed source said.

The Commerce Department on Wednesday said the U.S. Gross Domestic Product (GDP) grew by 5.6 percent in the first quarter of 1997. The GDP price index rose 2.7 percent, with the implicit price deflator gaining 2.3 percent.
The numbers were the first set of growth data for the period and are expected to be revised twice before the final figures are announced.
"I would be very surprised to see that number persist throughout the whole year," a third Fed source told Reuters.

"Not because of any sort of the economy going into the tank or something, but I think that there was a burst in the first quarter, and I think that succeeding quarters -- even if the economy stays fundamentally healthy -- would probably be less than that," the source added.
Some Fed sources said driving forces behind strong consumer spending were still not totally clear.
They added, however, the combination of healthy consumer spending, continued tight labor markets and a firm pace of growth might suggest Americans are feeling more confident about their jobs.

"It's not clear what factors are driving that (strong consumer spending). But maybe consumers didn't feel all that confident in 1996 and ended saving up their consumer durable purchases," the second Fed source added.
The indication is relevant because many economists inside and outside the Federal Reserve believe job insecurity has been one of the main factors holding back workers from demanding higher pay.
One of the Fed sources also said a downward revision of the strong 5.6 percent GDP growth rate was possible.
"There might be (revisions). Frequently in the past when you get such an anomalous quarter like that, when you come with a revision, the number is adjusted downward," the source said.
